stories.headline: Federal Judge Orders Trump Administration to Restore National Park Exhibits Removed Under History Executive Order
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction Friday ordering the Trump administration to restore exhibits and displays removed from national parks, museums, and landmarks under an executive order directing sites not to display elements that "inappropriately disparage Americans past or living." U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley wrote that the administration sought "to rewrite the Nation's history with a white-out pen" and ordered a halt to any additional changes, along with weekly status reports on compliance.

The ruling responds to a February lawsuit filed by conservation and historical organizations over National Park Service policies that resulted in the removal of dozens of exhibits covering slavery, climate change, and other topics. Among the changes challenged were the removal of exhibits at Philadelphia's Independence National Historical Park documenting the lives of nine enslaved people held by George Washington, the removal of a sign at Sunset Crater Volcano National Monument, and the stripping of labor history films from the Lowell National Historical Park in Massachusetts.

President Trump signed the executive order "restoring truth and sanity to American history" last year, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum subsequently directed the removal of "improper partisan ideology" from federally controlled public exhibits. Supporters of the administration's policy argued the changes promoted a unifying national narrative, while critics, including the National Parks Conservation Association, called the removals an attempt to erase historically accurate information from public view.

The injunction represents a significant legal setback for the administration's cultural and historical policy agenda. The Interior Department had not responded to requests for comment as of Saturday. The ruling could have broad implications for how the administration applies the executive order across the federal museum and monument system.

stories.headline: OpenAI Hit With Multistate Attorney General Probe Over User Safety as IPO Looms
stories.summary:
OpenAI received subpoenas from a coalition of state attorneys general as part of a multistate investigation into whether the company's ChatGPT chatbot poses harm to users, the company confirmed Saturday. The probe arrives days after OpenAI filed preliminary IPO paperwork with federal securities regulators, setting up a significant legal and regulatory cloud over one of the most anticipated public offerings in the technology sector.

The investigation follows mounting legal pressure on the company over ChatGPT's behavior in crisis situations. A Canadian lawsuit filed Thursday blames the chatbot for a teenager's suicide, while Florida's attorney general sued OpenAI earlier in June after two separate shootings in which alleged gunmen were reported to have consulted ChatGPT while planning their crimes. OpenAI stated its models had directed the individuals involved to seek mental health support and that it cooperated with law enforcement in the shooting cases.

OpenAI said it takes the attorneys general's concerns seriously and will respond "constructively," pointing to existing safeguards including protective features for minors and users in distress. The company faces scrutiny on multiple fronts: European regulators have separately investigated Elon Musk's rival Grok chatbot over antisemitic content, and the Trump administration this week ordered Anthropic to restrict overseas access to two of its AI models for national security reasons.

The multistate probe underscores the growing political and legal pressure on AI companies as they move toward public markets. How governments should regulate AI's potential harms has become an increasingly prominent policy debate, with the OpenAI investigation representing one of the most direct enforcement actions yet taken by state-level authorities against a leading AI firm.

stories.headline: Franco-German Fighter Jet Program Collapses, Raising Questions About Europe's Defense Ambitions
stories.summary:
Plans to build a joint European sixth-generation fighter jet at the center of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) program have officially collapsed, the countries confirmed this week, ending what had been billed as a cornerstone of European military cooperation. The program, estimated to cost 100 billion euros, foundered on fundamental disagreements between French manufacturer Dassault Aviation and European aerospace group Airbus over aircraft design — France sought a carrier-capable multirole jet while Germany envisioned a different platform, one that even questioned the necessity of a pilot.

The failure was widely anticipated by defense analysts, who noted the industrial incompatibilities between the two firms had been apparent since the program's announcement in 2017. French officials placed partial blame on Berlin for being unable to pressure Airbus toward compromise, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz acknowledged the companies' failure to cooperate but expressed optimism about preserving other elements of FCAS, including an envisioned "combat cloud" network and unmanned drone wingmen.

The collapse comes at a precarious moment for European defense policy, as the continent recalibrates its security architecture amid a diminished U.S. commitment to NATO under President Trump and the ongoing war in Ukraine. France is expected to pursue a domestically built successor aircraft, drawing on its long tradition of independent aviation development, while Germany may seek separate multinational partnerships or alternative procurement solutions.

Defense experts say the episode exposes the limits of multinational military-industrial cooperation in Europe and raises broader questions about whether the continent can develop sovereign next-generation defense capabilities. The surviving elements of FCAS — drones and the combat cloud — face their own uncertain future without the flagship aircraft program to anchor the initiative.

stories.headline: Restaurants in World Cup Host Cities Add Automatic 20% Gratuities for International Visitors
stories.summary:
Restaurants in several FIFA World Cup host cities, including Kansas City, Atlanta, and Philadelphia, are adding automatic 20% gratuities to customer bills during the tournament, citing concerns that international visitors from countries without strong tipping cultures may unknowingly undercompensate workers. The Missouri Restaurant Association had advised Kansas City establishments to adopt the policy, and similar moves are now spreading to other host cities as the tournament gets underway.

Operators implementing the surcharge say transparency is paramount, with notices being posted on menus and servers instructed to inform guests. "We don't want the servers or bartenders or the tipped employees to have to explain what the tipping custom is," said Ben Fileccia of the Pennsylvania Restaurant & Lodging Association, adding that pre-disclosed automatic gratuities make for a "smoother transaction."

Not everyone is supportive of the approach. Industry analyst David Henkes of Technomic cautioned that mandatory gratuities risk fueling consumer frustration at a time when restaurant traffic is already declining. "Anything that is perceived to increase the cost does risk some consumer backlash, particularly if it's not well-publicized or if consumers feel there's an expectation to tip on top of the automatic tip," he told Fox News Digital.

The debate reflects broader tensions in American tipping culture, which has faced increasing scrutiny from consumers unhappy with proliferating surcharges and fees. The World Cup, which opened in Los Angeles this weekend, is expected to bring millions of international visitors to the United States through the summer, making the question of tipping customs an unusually prominent point of contact between American service industry norms and global consumer expectations.

stories.headline: Update: Thousands Rally in Belfast and Glasgow to Condemn Anti-Immigrant Rioting
stories.summary:
Thousands of demonstrators gathered Saturday outside Belfast City Hall to denounce nights of violent anti-immigrant rioting that followed the arrest of a 30-year-old Sudanese man on attempted murder charges stemming from a stabbing that left another man partly blind. Masked groups had set fire to homes believed to house immigrants, torched a bus, and hurled bricks, bottles, and firebombs at police, injuring 12 officers and leaving more than two dozen people homeless.

Saturday's peaceful counter-rallies marked a significant shift in the public mood. Demonstrators carried signs reading "The problem is evil and violence not race" and "Your racism is not patriotism." One speaker told the crowd that a single violent act by a non-white person had been enough to "rekindle the fire of racism" — a warning about how quickly far-right networks were able to mobilize.

In Glasgow, an anti-racism group also rallied thousands in the city center, where earlier in the week disorder had targeted minorities and forced a mosque into lockdown. A smaller contingent of counter-protesters was observed making Nazi salutes and shouting anti-Muslim chants before being drowned out by chants of "Nazi scum off our streets."

British officials and the stabbing victim's own family had called for calm throughout the week. The episodes have reignited debate across the United Kingdom about immigration policy, far-right radicalization online, and the speed with which communal violence can erupt following high-profile crimes.

stories.headline: U.S. Vaccine Policy at Crossroads as RFK Jr. Faces Political Backlash Over HHS Moves
stories.summary:
A series of decisions expected over the coming months will reshape U.S. vaccine policy for years, with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at the center of a widening political battle. Kennedy came into office pledging to restore public trust in vaccines and to apply greater scrutiny to the pharmaceutical industry, but his most aggressive actions have drawn charges from public health experts and mainstream medical organizations that he is spreading misinformation and amplifying debunked theories.

Supporters of Kennedy argue that independent review of vaccine safety data is long overdue and that public skepticism of health institutions — accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic — demands a more transparent regulatory approach. Critics, including many former FDA and CDC officials, contend that Kennedy's moves risk undermining vaccination rates at a time when measles and other preventable diseases are resurging.

The decisions before HHS in the near term include potential changes to the childhood immunization schedule, the future of certain vaccine liability protections, and how the government communicates risk-benefit data to the public. Each carries significant implications for pharmaceutical manufacturers, state health departments, and millions of American families.

The political divide over Kennedy's tenure reflects broader tensions within the Republican coalition, where vaccine skepticism has grown while traditional public health conservatives push back against what they see as a dangerous departure from evidence-based policy.

stories.headline: NBA Finals Star James Harden Arrested in Houston on Misdemeanor Weapons Charge
stories.summary:
Cleveland Cavaliers guard James Harden was arrested in the early hours of Saturday morning in Houston, Texas, on a misdemeanor charge of unlawful carrying of a weapon, according to court records. Police stopped the vehicle Harden was driving through downtown Houston shortly before 4 a.m. and observed a handgun in the cup holder of his Mercedes. Harden was traveling with four other occupants at the time.

Harden, an 11-time NBA All-Star, was released from the Harris County jail on a $100 bond. The charge is a misdemeanor under Texas law. No details were provided about whether any of the other occupants faced charges.

The arrest comes during the NBA Finals, in which the Cavaliers are competing. The timing and circumstances — a high-profile athlete stopped with a visible weapon in a vehicle in the early morning hours — drew immediate attention across sports media. It was not immediately clear whether the NBA or the Cavaliers organization planned to comment.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Calls Iranian Negotiators 'Very Dishonorable' as Nuclear Deal Talks Strain
stories.summary:
President Trump sharply criticized Iranian negotiators on Friday, calling them "very dishonorable people" and rejecting leaked deal terms, introducing new turbulence into ongoing U.S.-Iran nuclear negotiations. The remarks came as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed that discussions over what Iran describes as "service fees" in the Strait of Hormuz remain part of the talks, while asserting that international law does not permit transit tolls on ships passing through the strategic waterway.

Araghchi said Iranian forces would continue to intervene in the Strait of Hormuz when necessary, complicating a key element of any potential agreement — the promised reopening of the waterway to normal commercial shipping. The Strait of Hormuz handles roughly 20 percent of global oil trade, and its status is a central concern for energy markets and U.S. allies in the region.

The exchange marks a significant deterioration in tone from earlier this week, when both sides signaled a deal could be signed within days. The breakdown in diplomatic language raises fresh questions about whether an agreement is achievable in the near term, with implications for U.S.-Israel tensions, ongoing Israeli strikes in Lebanon, and global oil prices.

Supporters of a diplomatic resolution argue a deal is essential to avoiding a wider regional conflict, while critics, including many congressional Republicans and Israeli officials, have expressed skepticism that Iran will honor any agreement and warn against concessions on uranium enrichment or Hormuz transit arrangements.

stories.headline: Update: France Buries Murdered Child as Police Failings Spark National Outcry; New Allegations Emerge Against Suspect's Father and Brother
stories.summary:
The town of Fleurance in southwestern France held a funeral Friday for Lyhanna, an 11-year-old girl murdered two weeks ago, as public anger intensified over a cascade of law enforcement failures that left her suspected killer free despite multiple prior warnings. Prime suspect Jérôme Barella, 41, had been reported to police nine months earlier for alleged repeated sexual abuse of a 10-year-old girl, yet was never questioned by investigators.

New details have deepened the scandal: French authorities confirmed that U.S. law enforcement had alerted French police to Barella's online activity suggesting access to child sexual abuse material as far back as 2023, a signal French authorities classified as "weak" and did not act upon. France's National Office for Minors said it receives approximately 300,000 such signals annually, a volume officials say strains investigative capacity.

The case has widened further with new allegations against Barella's family. His brother Yannick was placed under formal investigation for rape following complaints by two women, one of whom was a minor at the time of the alleged offense, after he was taken into custody this week when he went to police to file a defamation complaint. The brothers' father, Joël Barella, 71, is also under investigation after prosecutors reopened a 2019 case alleging sexual abuse of a partner's granddaughter.

The case has triggered a broader national debate in France over the handling of sex crimes against women and minors, with officials facing accusations of systemic negligence. Mayors across the Gers region ordered flags flown at half-mast as residents gathered outside town halls in solidarity with the victim's family.

stories.headline: Canada's Carney Urges Middle Powers to Form 'Third Path' Away from U.S. Ahead of G7 Summit
stories.summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney intensified his effort to reorient Canada toward Europe on Saturday, meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin and telling an audience at Trinity College that middle-power nations should not "compete for favor" with the United States but instead combine their strength to forge an independent path. The remarks came one day before the G7 summit in France, where Carney is expected to coordinate with European leaders on trade and defense policy.

Carney noted that the combined population and economy of Canada and the European Union is more than twice that of the United States, and that their collective defense spending is double China's. He described Canada as "the most European of non-European countries" and said the two sides are transforming their cooperation across critical minerals, defense procurement, and financial sectors. Canada earlier this year became the first non-European member of the EU's SAFE defense procurement mechanism.

The remarks carry immediate diplomatic weight as a scheduled July 1 review of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement approaches. Carney acknowledged that Washington has signaled it does not want to alter the fundamental architecture of the trade deal, a position he presented as clarifying rather than conciliatory. U.S. President Trump is not currently scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Carney at the G7, according to a senior U.S. administration official.

The pivot reflects broader tension between Canada and the Trump administration over tariffs and sovereignty. Supporters of Carney's approach argue that diversifying alliances strengthens Canada's negotiating hand; critics, including some Canadian business groups, warn that antagonizing Washington risks economic harm given the depth of bilateral trade ties.

stories.headline: California Attorney General's Office Warned Local Police That Welfare Checks on Migrant Children Could Violate Sanctuary Law
stories.summary:
California's sanctuary state policies have become the focus of a new legal and political conflict after the state attorney general's office warned local police in El Cajon that conducting welfare checks on unaccompanied migrant children using contact information provided by federal immigration authorities could violate state law. The warning has become a central element of a lawsuit brought by El Cajon against California's sanctuary policies.

El Cajon City Councilman Steve Goble said federal Homeland Security officials in February 2025 shared a list of 52 unaccompanied migrant children with addresses in the city and asked whether local police could verify their safety. Goble wrote to Attorney General Rob Bonta's office seeking legal guidance before dispatching officers. Bonta's office responded that sharing information with federal immigration authorities or acting on federally provided data could conflict with the California Values Act, the state's primary sanctuary law.

El Cajon Mayor Bill Wells accused state officials of prioritizing ideological commitments over child safety. "What they basically want to say is, 'Because our narrative is so important, and protecting illegal aliens is so important, that, yeah, if a few kids get sex trafficked along the way," Wells told Fox News Digital. "These are real people. These are real children."

Defenders of California's sanctuary framework argue that allowing local police to act on federal immigration data would undermine the trust between immigrant communities and law enforcement, making crime victims and witnesses less likely to cooperate with police. The dispute highlights a recurring tension between state immigration policies and local governments that argue those policies restrict their ability to protect vulnerable residents.

stories.headline: World Cup Opening Ceremony Launches Tournament in Los Angeles
stories.summary:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup opened with a high-energy ceremony at the Los Angeles Coliseum on Friday, featuring performances by Katy Perry, Future, Tyla, Anitta, and LISA of K-pop group Blackpink. The United States then faced Paraguay in the host nation's first World Cup match on home soil since 1994. Earlier in the day, Canada hosted its own ceremony in Toronto with Alanis Morissette and Michael Bublé performing ahead of Canada's match against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The tournament is the largest in World Cup history, featuring 48 nations competing across venues in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Canada earned its first-ever World Cup point with a draw against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hollywood celebrities including Paris Hilton, Owen Wilson, and Sofia Vergara attended the Los Angeles match, and Ted Lasso actor Jason Sudeikis participated in a flag parade on the pitch.

Fans traveled from across the country and the world for the opening matches, with some reporting ticket prices of $1,900 or more. The event drew significant crowds despite ongoing geopolitical tensions that have shadowed the tournament's lead-up, including disputes over referee eligibility and U.S. trade relations with co-host nations Mexico and Canada.

The 2026 World Cup represents a major moment for soccer's profile in the United States, with organizers and broadcasters anticipating record viewership. The tournament runs through July.

stories.headline: Nevada and Maine Hold Primary Elections; Ford Wins Democratic Gubernatorial Nod in Nevada
stories.summary:
Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford won the Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday, setting up a November general election against Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo in one of the country's most closely watched battleground races. Ford, who has emphasized his working-class upbringing and reliance on public assistance as a young single father, has been positioning himself as a champion for blue-collar workers in a state where economic concerns are expected to dominate the race.

Lombardo, who easily secured the Republican nomination, issued a statement citing progress on job growth, education, and public safety while acknowledging more work remains. His allies have sought to portray Ford as out of touch and absent from the state during his tenure as attorney general. Analysts expect the race to hinge largely on voter assessments of Nevada's economy.

In Maine, Republican Bobby Charles, a former State Department official under President George W. Bush, held a sizable lead in the GOP gubernatorial primary but remained well short of 50 percent under the state's ranked-choice voting system. The Democratic primary for Maine's Second Congressional District — the seat held by centrist Rep. Jared Golden — remained competitive in a three-way race, with state Sen. Joe Baldacci holding a narrow lead.

The primaries represent an early test of both parties' strength heading into the November midterm elections, with control of several governorships and congressional seats in play. Nevada is considered a true toss-up in the general election.

stories.headline: Pentagon Releases Fourth Batch of Declassified UFO Videos Showing Unexplained Orbs
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Defense released four previously classified videos on Friday showing bright orbs moving through the sky over the northeastern United States, the government's third release of UFO-related footage and documents. The clips, which were originally sent to the FBI, were recorded between 2021 and 2025 and correspond with other eyewitness reports from the same general region, though the Pentagon declined to specify exact locations.

The Defense Department characterized the materials as originating from 'unresolved cases,' meaning investigators were 'unable to make a definitive determination on the nature of the observed phenomena.' The release is part of a broader ongoing effort to declassify government records related to unidentified aerial phenomena, a process that has accelerated under congressional pressure over the past several years.

The videos do not include additional analysis or conclusions about what the objects might be. Officials have previously said that the declassification effort is intended to improve transparency and public trust, while stopping short of making claims about extraterrestrial origins.

stories.headline: Update: Defense Lawyers in Charlie Kirk Murder Case Seek to Bar Death Penalty Over Prosecutor Media Comments
stories.summary:
Attorneys for Tyler Robinson, the 23-year-old Utah man charged with the September 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, asked a judge Friday to block prosecutors from seeking the death penalty, citing what they described as improper media statements about ballistics evidence. The defense argued that prosecutors violated a court-imposed gag order by speaking publicly about a bullet fragment that federal testing was unable to conclusively link to the rifle investigators believe was used in the killing.

Prosecutors defended their media appearances as necessary to correct what they characterized as widespread misinformation and unsubstantiated conspiracy theories — including claims of a second shooter or that Kirk's death was staged — that spread after the preliminary ballistics finding became public. Deputy Utah County Attorney Christopher Ballard argued in court filings that attorneys have a right to respond to prejudicial media coverage and that he spoke only in general terms about how ballistics testing can be inconclusive.

The defense countered that Ballard's statements went beyond general commentary and were designed to influence public perception of the case before trial. Robinson, who has not yet entered a plea, faces an aggravated murder charge. Prosecutors have stated their intent to seek the death penalty if he is convicted. Separately, authorities say DNA consistent with Robinson's was found on the trigger of the rifle, a fired cartridge casing, two unfired cartridges, and a towel used to wrap the weapon.

The hearing adds a new legal complication to a case that has attracted intense national attention since Kirk was shot in the neck while addressing a large crowd at Utah Valley University. A ruling on the defense motion could significantly affect the prosecution's sentencing options.

stories.headline: ICE Obtains Local Voter Registration Files in Two Counties in Noncitizen Voting Probe
stories.summary:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators have obtained individual voter files directly from local election officials in two counties — one in Texas and one in North Carolina — according to emails shared with Axios. The action represents a new phase in the Trump administration's multi-agency effort to investigate alleged noncitizen voting, going beyond federal databases and reaching into state and local election systems.

President Trump has long claimed that millions of noncitizens vote illegally in U.S. elections and has used that assertion to explain his loss in the 2016 popular vote. Supporters of the effort argue it is a legitimate law enforcement exercise to protect election integrity, while critics warn that ICE accessing voter rolls sets a troubling precedent that could chill voter registration and blur the line between immigration enforcement and election administration.

The disclosure raises legal and constitutional questions about the appropriate role of immigration authorities in accessing election records, which are administered under state and local law. Election law advocates on the left argue the move could amount to voter intimidation and a federal overreach into state-controlled systems; administration allies contend existing law permits such inquiries as part of a lawful investigation into potential federal crimes.

stories.headline: Update: Anthropic Suspends Claude Fable 5 AI Model Worldwide After U.S. Government Security Order
stories.summary:
Anthropic has been ordered by U.S. national security authorities to suspend access to its most powerful AI model, Claude Fable 5, just days after its public release. The company said it was directed to bar foreign nationals from using the tool, and because it could not reliably enforce that restriction for individual users, it disabled the model entirely for all customers globally, including a related model called Mythos 5.

U.S. authorities told Anthropic they had become aware of a method for "jailbreaking" Fable 5 — bypassing its safety restrictions in ways that could allow hackers to exploit computer systems. Anthropic said it reviewed a demonstration of the technique and found the vulnerabilities to be relatively minor and already discoverable through other publicly available AI models, suggesting the company believes the government's concerns may be overstated.

The suspension adds to an already fraught relationship between Anthropic and the Trump administration. The Defense Department previously designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk" — the first time such a label, historically reserved for foreign adversaries, was applied to a U.S. company. Anthropic is currently suing the Pentagon over that designation. A federal judge has ruled the directive unenforceable in the meantime, allowing government-adjacent organizations to continue using Anthropic's other tools.

stories.headline: Justice Department Clears $111 Billion Warner Bros. Discovery Sale to Paramount
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice has approved Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing a major antitrust hurdle for what would be one of the largest media mergers in history. The DOJ said it conducted a "rigorous" review and found the deal unlikely to harm competition or consumers, and predicted it would actually increase competition across the media landscape.

The combined company would control an enormous portfolio of media assets, including CNN, HBO, Warner Bros. film studios, DC Studios, CBS, Showtime, Nickelodeon, and multiple cable networks. The deal has drawn opposition from more than 1,400 Hollywood actors, directors, and filmmakers who signed an open letter warning it would reduce jobs, limit creative opportunities, raise costs, and shrink choices for audiences.

The merger is not yet final. California Attorney General Rob Bonta has been reviewing the deal and previously expressed concern that further consolidation would harm the entertainment industry; a spokesperson said the state's investigation remains open. The deal has also attracted scrutiny because Paramount is led by David Ellison, son of Oracle's Larry Ellison, a major donor to President Trump — raising questions among critics about whether political considerations influenced the DOJ's approval.

stories.headline: Shooting in Downtown Midland, Texas Kills at Least One; Suspect Dead
stories.summary:
At least one person was killed and others injured in a shooting in downtown Midland, Texas on Friday, Mayor Lori Blong announced at a press conference. The suspect, who had barricaded themselves inside a building following the shooting, was subsequently confirmed dead.

Midland police and emergency services responded to the active-shooter situation in the city's downtown area. Authorities provided limited details as the situation was still developing at the time of initial reports. The incident drew coverage from more than a dozen national news outlets.

Midland, a West Texas city of roughly 130,000 people and a center of the Permian Basin oil industry, was the site of a mass shooting in August 2019 in which a gunman killed seven people and wounded more than 20 others in a rampage across the city and neighboring Odessa. Authorities have not yet released information on a motive or the identities of those involved in Friday's incident.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Deal Near Signing as Israel Strikes Lebanon, Hormuz Reopening Promised
stories.summary:
Iran's foreign minister said Friday that a deal to end hostilities with the United States is close to finalization and would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting a U.S. blockade of Iran. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who helped mediate the agreement, confirmed a Memorandum of Understanding had been agreed and awaited finalizing. However, Iran's foreign minister acknowledged that the Supreme National Security Council had not yet reached a collective decision, saying "supporters and opponents" exist within Iran's top security body.

President Trump said Thursday he had cancelled scheduled strikes against Iran because negotiators had reached a "great settlement," but then disputed details published by Iranian media, saying the leaked terms "bear no relation to the truth." U.S. officials confirmed some elements of the deal, stating that economic benefits for Iran would be contingent on Tehran meeting its obligations. The agreement is also said to envision an end to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict in Lebanon, though Lebanon's inclusion has been disputed in earlier reports.

Israel carried out fresh airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Friday after ordering residents to evacuate roughly 20 locations, with at least one person killed in the Tyre district town of Marrakeh. The strikes came hours after Iran's foreign minister outlined deal terms, underscoring the fragility of the broader ceasefire framework. Iran has previously warned Israel it could resume hostilities if attacks on Hezbollah do not stop.

The ongoing conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, has closed the Strait of Hormuz and trapped an estimated 20,000 seafarers in the war zone. BBC Verify analysis of satellite imagery found Iran has damaged 20 U.S. military sites since the war began, more than publicly acknowledged. The deal's nuclear components — long a central Western concern — are reportedly deferred to later negotiations.

stories.headline: U.S. Military Kills Tren de Aragua Gang Leader Niño Guerrero in Airstrike
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that U.S. Southern Command carried out a lethal airstrike killing Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, known as Niño Guerrero, the longtime leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Trump posted footage of the strike on social media and said the operation was "coordinated closely" with Venezuelan authorities, who confirmed their participation in what they called a "joint operation." The Trump administration had previously designated Tren de Aragua a foreign terrorist organization and accused it of engaging in "irregular warfare" against the United States.

Tren de Aragua originated as a prison gang in Venezuela that Guerrero transformed into a transnational criminal organization with operations in at least nine countries, including the United States. Under his leadership, the group expanded into Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Chile, diversifying from extorting migrants into sex trafficking, contract killing, and kidnapping. The U.S. State Department had offered millions of dollars for information leading to his arrest or capture.

The killing comes amid a significant reshaping of U.S.-Venezuela relations. In January, American forces seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in a raid; Guerrero Flores had been named as a co-conspirator in Maduro's U.S. indictment. Since Maduro's removal, the U.S. has worked to build ties with his successor, Delcy Rodríguez, including lifting sanctions and pursuing collaboration on Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Guerrero had a long history of escaping accountability, including bribing a guard to escape prison in 2012 and evading capture again in 2023 when Maduro sent 11,000 soldiers to retake the Tocorón Prison — which Guerrero had transformed into a compound complete with a zoo, nightclub, and swimming pool. His death marks the most significant targeted strike against a Latin American criminal organization's leadership under the Trump administration.

stories.headline: Update: FISA Section 702 Expires as Congress Deadlocks Over Trump Intelligence Nominee
stories.summary:
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, one of the U.S. government's most powerful foreign surveillance tools, lapsed this weekend after Congress failed to reauthorize it. Democrats blocked extension votes in both chambers in protest of President Trump's nomination of Housing Secretary Bill Pulte to temporarily oversee the nation's intelligence services. The standoff leaves the fate of ongoing intelligence collection in legal uncertainty, with the law's expiration coming days before the 2026 World Cup, which U.S. security officials have flagged as a heightened terrorism target.

Lawmakers and legal experts are divided on the practical consequences of the lapse. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) argued that thousands of existing FISA certifications remain valid and that the expiration does not immediately end U.S. surveillance of foreign terrorists. However, Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, warned the situation was "a high-risk proposition," raising the possibility that telecom and tech companies such as Google could decline to cooperate with intelligence requests without explicit congressional authorization.

Section 702 allows the government to collect communications of foreign nationals abroad using U.S. infrastructure, though it also incidentally captures communications of Americans in contact with foreign suspects — a provision that has long troubled privacy advocates in both parties. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) placed blame on the Trump administration, saying it had "tossed a hand grenade into the middle of sensitive negotiations" by installing Pulte. Republicans countered that Democrats were endangering national security for political reasons.

The program had previously been credited with disrupting domestic terror plots. A resolution is not expected soon, as Trump has shown no indication he will withdraw the Pulte nomination, and Democrats have not signaled any willingness to relent without a concession.

stories.headline: Switzerland Votes Sunday on Unprecedented Referendum to Cap Population at 10 Million
stories.summary:
Swiss voters will go to the polls Sunday on a proposal backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party to constitutionally cap the country's population at 10 million residents before 2050, with mandatory government action once the population reaches 9.5 million. Proposed measures to enforce the cap could include limiting asylum grants and ending family reunification for foreign residents. Switzerland's population has grown from 7.3 million in 2002 to 9.1 million today, with 27 percent of residents being foreign nationals.

The Swiss government, all major opposition parties, business groups, and trade unions have united against the measure, calling it a "chaos initiative" that would deprive hospitals and hotels of essential workers and damage Switzerland's carefully maintained bilateral relations with the European Union, of which it is not a member. Supporters argue unchecked immigration has driven a housing shortage, overcrowded trains, and rising healthcare costs. No other country has attempted a hard constitutional cap on population.

Polling shows the vote is extremely close, with roughly 52 percent of respondents opposed and 45 percent in favor, while a significant share of voters remain undecided. The outcome could have significant implications for Switzerland's relationship with the EU, its labor market, and its reputation as a destination for international workers and talent.
